title: Largest Sum of a Contiguous Run
statement:
You get an integer array nums. A run is a block of one or more neighbouring elements, such as nums[2..5].

Return the largest sum any run can have. The run cannot be empty, so if every number is negative the answer is still negative.

examples.why: The run 4, −1, 5. Stopping at the first negative number gives only 4 (or 5 alone); crossing the −1 pays because the 5 behind it is bigger. Adding up only the positives gives 11, but those are not neighbours.
Every number is negative, so the best run is the single largest element. Answering 0 would mean an empty run, which is not allowed.
The run 3, 4. Carrying the 5 along is a mistake: 5 − 7 is negative, and any run that starts with that dead weight is beaten by the same run without it.

hints: Fix where the run ends. What is the best run that ends exactly at index i?
The best run ending at i is either nums[i] alone, or nums[i] glued onto the best run ending at i − 1. When is gluing a bad idea?
Glue only while the run behind you has a positive sum. Keep the best run ending here, and the best value seen anywhere. Start both at nums[0], not at 0.

explain.intuition:
Walk left to right and keep one number: cur, the best sum of a run that ends at the current index. At each new element you have only two choices: start fresh with nums[i], or extend the run you are carrying. Extending is right exactly when cur is positive.

This is the shape every greedy proof takes: show that the greedy choice never hurts. Take any run that ends at i and starts earlier. Split it into a prefix and the rest. If the prefix sums to something negative, cutting it off gives a run with a strictly bigger sum. So the best run ending at i never carries a negative prefix, and that is all the rule "drop cur when it goes negative" does. Nothing is thrown away that could ever have helped. The answer is the largest cur seen, because the best run overall has to end somewhere.
steps: For each later element x: cur = max(x, cur + x). This drops the old run when it would only drag x down.
pitfalls: Starting best at 0. On an all-negative array like [-6, -2, -8] you return 0, the sum of an empty run, instead of −2.
Resetting the run as soon as you meet a negative number. In [-3, 4, -1, 5, -9, 2] the −1 is worth crossing. Reset only when the whole carried sum is negative.
Updating best only when you reset. The best run can end anywhere, so compare after every element.

solutions.title: Every start, growing end
solutions.idea: For each start, extend the end one step at a time and keep a running sum. Every run is checked once.

solutions.title: Prefix sums minus the lowest earlier prefix
solutions.idea: The run i..j sums to prefix[j + 1] − prefix[i]. For each end, subtract the smallest prefix seen before it. Same trick as the best single trade.

solutions.title: Carry the run while it helps (Kadane)
solutions.idea: Keep the best run ending here. A run with a negative sum can only hurt what comes next, so drop it and start fresh.

followups: Return the start and end index of the best run as well. Which run do you return on a tie?
The array is circular: a run may wrap from the end back to the start. How do you reuse this algorithm?
Solve it with divide and conquer in O(n log n). What does each half have to report to its parent?
